overview.bigIdea: Numbers are for playing, puzzling and discovering. This chapter trains **computational thinking**: follow a set procedure (a routine) carefully, step by step, and look for what happens.

ladder.a: Compare each cell with left, right (top, bottom)

languages.name: Follow a routine
languages.text: Kaprekar and Collatz: one careful step at a time.

languages.name: Estimate
languages.text: Round to friendly numbers to judge if an answer is sensible.

plan.text: Kaprekar and Collatz lessons – practise 3 numbers each with full working (4-mark questions).
Palindrome puzzles, smallest/largest numbers, digit sums.
Check knowledge quiz; revisit after 1, 3, 7 days.

lessons.title: Numbers tell us things & supercells
lessons.hook: Children in a line each call out the number of **taller neighbours** they have. Numbers can carry information – and in a table, a number that beats all its neighbours becomes a **supercell**.

core.def: Each child says 0, 1 or 2 – how many of the children next to them are taller. End children have only one neighbour.
A cell whose number is **greater than all its neighbouring cells**.
In a row: left and right. In a grid: left, right, top and bottom.
Always a supercell. The smallest number can never be one (in a table with 2 or more cells).

explain: To mark supercells, go cell by cell and compare only with **direct neighbours**, not the whole table.
Maximum supercells in a row: alternate big–small–big … so every other cell wins.

steps: 789 > 345 (only neighbour) → supercell. 457, 123, 345 are smaller than a neighbour.

mistakes: Comparing with cells that are not neighbours.
Forgetting that end cells have only one neighbour.
Thinking only the biggest number can be a supercell.
lessons.tip: Write a small ✓ or ✗ above each cell as you check – examiners like to see the comparison.
lessons.memory: Supercell = local champion: beat your neighbours, not everyone.
examAsk: Colour the supercells in a table.
Fill a table so that given cells are supercells.
Can the smallest number be a supercell? Why?

cards.q: Is the largest number always a supercell?

diagram.caption: Model paper Q27a row – find the supercells.

lessons.title: Number line, digits and digit sums
lessons.hook: How many 3-digit numbers are there? Not 999! From 100 to 999 there are 900. Thinking carefully about **digits** avoids silly slips.

core.def: 1-digit: 9 · 2-digit: 90 · 3-digit: 900 · 4-digit: 9000 · 5-digit: 90,000.
Add the digits: 68 → 6 + 8 = 14. Different numbers can have the same digit sum (68, 176, 545).
Use few digits, largest digits at the end: digit sum 14 → 59.
Largest digits first, then zeros: 5-digit, digit sum 14 → 95000.
Place a number by its distance from the nearest marks: 2754 is between 2000 and 3000, nearer 3000.

explain: Counting a digit: from 1 to 100 the digit 7 appears 10 times in the units place and 10 times in the tens place – 20 times.
Commas help reading large numbers: 36,109 (Indian system: 1,10,000).

example.q: Find the smallest number and the largest 5-digit number whose digit sum is 14.
steps: Smallest: as few digits as possible → 2 digits; smaller digit first: 5 and 9 → 59.
Largest 5-digit: put 9 first, then 14 − 9 = 5, then zeros → 95000.

mistakes: Writing 95 instead of 59 for the smallest.
Forgetting zeros can be used to fill places.
lessons.tip: For smallest/largest questions, write the place-value boxes (tth th h t u) and fill them one by one.
lessons.memory: Smallest: few digits, small first. Largest: big digits first.
examAsk: Smallest/largest number with a given digit sum.
How many times does a digit appear from 1 to 100?

lessons.title: Palindromes, clock and calendar numbers
lessons.hook: Read 12321 backwards – still 12321! Numbers that read the same both ways are **palindromes**, and they hide in clocks (11:11) and dates (11/02/2011) too.

core.def: Reads the same from left to right and right to left: 66, 848, 575, 1111.
Add a number to its reverse and repeat until you get a palindrome: 39 + 93 = 132, 132 + 231 = 363.

explain: A palindrome is decided by its outer digits pairing up: in a 5-digit palindrome, digit 1 = digit 5 and digit 2 = digit 4; the middle digit is free.
Mystery: starting with 196 and reversing-and-adding has never been shown to give a palindrome – nobody knows!

example.q: What is the sum and difference of the smallest and largest 5-digit palindromes? (Model paper Q29, 3 marks)

mistakes: Writing 10000 as the smallest 5-digit palindrome (it is not a palindrome).
Forgetting the middle digit can be anything.
lessons.tip: In palindrome puzzles, draw 5 boxes (tth th h t u), mark equal pairs with arrows, then fill in the clues.
lessons.memory: Mirror the digits: first = last, second = second-last.
examAsk: Sum/difference of smallest and largest palindromes.
Next palindromic time on a clock.

lessons.title: Kaprekar’s magic number 6174
lessons.hook: In 1949, **D. R. Kaprekar**, a mathematics teacher in Devlali, Maharashtra, found magic: take any 4-digit number (not all digits the same), repeat ‘largest minus smallest’, and you always land on **6174**.

core.def: A = largest number from the digits, B = smallest number from the digits, C = A − B. Repeat with C.
At least two different digits (3333 gives 0).
Keep 4 digits: 378 is written 0378 → A = 8730, B = 0378.
Reaches 495.

explain: Count **rounds** = number of subtractions until you get 6174. It is never more than 7 for 4-digit numbers.
Neat working wins marks: one line per round, A − B = C.

example.q: How many rounds does 3524 take to reach 6174? (Model paper Q37a)

mistakes: Dropping the zero: using 378 instead of 0378.
Subtraction slips – check by adding C + B = A.
Using a number with all digits the same.
lessons.tip: Always check each subtraction by adding back: B + C should give A. It takes 10 seconds and saves marks.
examAsk: Number of rounds for a 4-digit number (or your birth year).
Carry out the routine for a 3-digit number.
Why must the digits not all be the same?

cards.a: A maths teacher from Devlali, Maharashtra.

lessons.title: Mental maths, patterns and estimation
lessons.hook: You don’t always need an exact answer. Paromita’s class has sections of 32, 29 and 35 – ‘about 100’ is good enough to plan. **Estimation** and smart grouping make mental maths fast.

core.def: Add equal numbers by multiplying: 5 × 40 + 5 × 50 = 450.
5-digit + 5-digit: sometimes 5-digit. 4-digit + 2-digit = 6-digit: never. 5-digit − 2-digit = 3-digit: never.
Round to friendly numbers, then calculate.

explain: To decide ‘always/sometimes/never’, test the **extreme** cases – the smallest and largest possible numbers.
Estimate first, then calculate. If the two are far apart, re-check.

example.q: Is ‘5-digit number − 2-digit number = 3-digit number’ always, sometimes or never true?
steps: Try the smallest 5-digit number and the largest 2-digit number: 10,000 − 99 = 9901.
Even the smallest possible result has 4 digits.

mistakes: Testing only one easy example and saying ‘always’.
Adding numbers one by one instead of grouping.
Treating an estimate as the exact answer.
lessons.tip: In ‘always/sometimes/never’, give one example (or the extreme case) as proof – that is what earns the mark.
lessons.memory: Test the edges: smallest and largest possible numbers.
examAsk: Find a quick way to add a pattern of numbers.

lessons.title: Collatz conjecture and number games
lessons.hook: Pick any number. If even, halve it; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Keep going … you always seem to reach **1**. Nobody in the world has proved it always happens – it is the famous unsolved **Collatz conjecture** (1937).

core.def: Even → ÷ 2. Odd → × 3 + 1. Repeat until 1.
A statement believed to be true but not yet proved.
Always reach 1 by halving (64 → 32 → … → 1).
Add 1, 2 or 3 each turn; first to 21 wins. Winning numbers: 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21 (4 apart).

explain: Collatz sequences can climb high before falling: 7 → 22 → 11 → 34 → 17 → 52 → 26 → 13 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1.
Winning strategy games work backwards from the target: if you can say 17, you can always reach 21.

example.q: Check whether the Collatz conjecture holds for 21. (Model paper Q35, 4 marks)

mistakes: Halving an odd number (giving a fraction).
lessons.tip: Write the rule at the top of your answer, then each step as ‘number → next’ with the operation. End with a conclusion sentence.
lessons.memory: Even → half. Odd → triple plus one.
examAsk: Write the Collatz sequence for a number and state if it reaches 1.
Why does the conjecture hold for powers of 2?
Find the winning strategy in a number game.

revision: Supercell: a number greater than all its neighbouring cells; the largest number always is one.
There are 9 one-digit, 90 two-digit, 900 three-digit, 9000 four-digit numbers.
Digit sum: add the digits. Smallest with digit sum 14 is 59; largest 5-digit is 95000.
Palindromes read the same both ways; smallest 5-digit 10001, largest 99999 (sum 110000, difference 89998).
Reverse-and-add usually produces a palindrome (196 is a mystery).
Kaprekar routine: largest − smallest, repeat; 4-digit numbers reach 6174, 3-digit reach 495.
Keep 4 digits in Kaprekar (0378) and check each subtraction by adding back.
Collatz: even → half, odd → × 3 + 1; conjecture: always reaches 1 (unproved since 1937).
Powers of 2 reach 1 just by halving.
Estimate by rounding; test ‘always/sometimes/never’ with extreme cases.

paper.what: Mark the supercells in a row
Sum and difference of smallest and largest 5-digit palindromes

sections.title: Routine questions (Kaprekar, Collatz)
items: One line per step: show A, B and A − B (or the Collatz operation).
Check each subtraction by adding back.
Finish with a sentence: ‘It takes 3 rounds’ / ‘The sequence reaches 1’.

sections.title: Digit puzzles
items: Draw place-value boxes (tth th h t u).
Mark which digits must be equal (palindromes).
Fill in clue by clue and check every clue at the end.

sections.title: Answer writing
items: Write the rule or definition in one line first, then apply it – rule lines earn marks even if the arithmetic slips.
Show every step on its own line (for example each division in a prime factorisation or each Kaprekar round).
Underline or box the final answer and write the unit (°, students, books) where there is one.
For ‘Give reason / Justify’ questions: state the rule, then show that the number or figure fits (or does not fit) it.

checklist: I can mark supercells in a row or grid.
I know how many n-digit numbers there are.
I can find smallest/largest numbers with a given digit sum.
I can solve palindrome puzzles and sums/differences.
I can run the Kaprekar routine and count rounds.
I can write a Collatz sequence and explain the conjecture.
I can decide always/sometimes/never with examples.

method: Built on proven learning methods: see it as a picture first, understand why it works, learn from worked examples, then test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
